blindComparison: A stranger picks the Ghost of Tsushima frame, and the reason is the shadows. In the reference, shadowed ground at golden hour is a saturated cool blue-violet sitting at roughly a fifth of the sunlit value, and every stone joint inside it is still readable. In `phone-hero-r9.png` the equivalent cast shadow at (1400,1010 100x40) measures mean RGB 5.3,4.2,3.6 with median luma 1.0 and surface detail 2.67, against sunlit flagstone 120 px away at (1150,830) measuring 65.0,44.4,32.8 with detail 9.63. That is a 46x value drop and 72% of the texture gone. Our shadows are not shadows, they are holes punched through the ground, and the eye reads that instantly at thumbnail size before it notices anything else in the frame. Second reason, same frame: the shadow boundary at x 880-960, y 770-800 is a hard staircase of 7-14 row blocks, so even the hole has a jagged 1980s edge.

findings.problem: Nothing fills shadow. Sky/ambient contribution to shadowed surfaces is effectively zero, and what little is there is warm rather than cool, so every shadowed region collapses to near-black warm brown with its surface texture destroyed. Measured: (a) `hero` cast shadow on flagstone at (1400,1010 100x40) = mean RGB 5.3,4.2,3.6, luma p50 1.0, detail 2.67; the adjacent sunlit flagstone at (1150,830 120x50) = 65.0,44.4,32.8, luma p50 46.4, detail 9.63 — a 46x value drop with 72% of the joint texture lost. A column scan at x=960 goes 40,40,40 (y=767) to 0,0,0 (y=770): the shadow bottoms out at literal RGB 0,0,0 on open ground in an exterior. (b) `sun` row scan at y=1040 crosses a ground shadow at x 934->949: lit sand 130,78,39 -> shadow 38,13,3. The blue channel falls from 30% of red to 8% of red, i.e. the shadow is WARMER than the key light, the exact inverse of a real golden hour. (c) `sun` backlit post at y=450: interior 46,12,2 and the anti-sun edge pixel at x=2285 is 30,11,7, while the sky it faces at x=2295 is 166,174,168 — a vertical face seeing half a luma-171 sky hemisphere renders at luma 7, a 24:1 ratio. (d) `valley` deepest corner (1900,900 300x150) = 26.3,14.6,5.5, still R:B = 4.8:1.
findings.why: This is the single largest gap to the reference. Tsushima and Sekiro both sell golden hour on the two-temperature split: warm key, cool sky-filled shade, with full material detail surviving in the shade. With no fill, objects stop having a shaded side and start having a black side, which is what makes a real-time frame read as a 2005 renderer. Every other item on this list is cosmetic next to it.
findings.fix: Shadowed exterior ground must land at roughly 18-25% of the sunlit value, not 2%, and must be measurably cooler than the key. Concrete target on `hero`: the box at (1400,1010 100x40) should measure mean luma between 9 and 13 (currently 1.0-ish at p50, mean RGB luma ~4.5) with detail >= 6.0 (currently 2.67), and its blue channel must be >= 90% of its red channel (currently 68%). On `sun`, the shadow at (940,1030) should read roughly 45,42,52 rather than 38,13,3 — same luma order, cool instead of warm. Verify by re-measuring those exact two boxes before and after; byte-identical numbers mean you edited a branch that does not draw those pixels.
findings.hypothesis: The shadow term may be multiplying the ambient/IBL contribution as well as the direct term, so the sky probe is being switched off inside shadow instead of remaining as fill. Disprove first by ablating: force the shadow factor to a constant 0.0 everywhere and measure whether the frame goes to black or settles at a non-zero ambient floor. If it settles above luma 8, this hypothesis is wrong and the fill is simply too dim / too warm, which is a different fix.

findings.problem: The cast shadow boundary is a hard rectangular staircase with no penumbra at all. Per-row measurement of the left edge of the black shadow region in `phone-hero-r9.png` (first pixel below luma 8, scanning x from 880): y=770..776 all hold x=959; y=777..783 all hold x=952; y=784..798 all hold x=936/937; y=799 jumps to x=907. So the silhouette advances in blocks 7 to 15 rows tall and 7 to 30 px wide, holding a constant x for up to 15 consecutive rows. The transition itself is 1-2 px wide (column x=960: 40,40,40 at y=767 -> 26,26,26 at y=768 -> 3,3,3 at y=769 -> 0,0,0 at y=770). Visible unaided in a 1:1 crop of (880,690 420x210) as a flight of black square steps running diagonally across the courtyard.
findings.why: A 15 px shadow-map texel on a shadow 10 m from camera is a resolution artefact a shipped title would never let through, and the total absence of penumbra growth means every shadow has the same infinitely-sharp edge regardless of how far the caster is from the ground. The brief's second priority is exactly this: contact hardening tight at the base, softening with distance. We currently have neither — just one hard aliased edge everywhere.
findings.fix: Two separate targets, both measurable on `phone-hero-r9.png`. (1) Kill the blocking: re-run the per-row left-edge scan over y=770..800 at x in [880,980]; no x value may repeat for more than 3 consecutive rows, and no row-to-row jump may exceed 6 px. (2) Add real penumbra: the luma transition across the shadow boundary on the column at x=960 near y=769 must span >= 6 px of monotonic intermediate values, and a shadow edge far from its caster must be measurably softer than one at a contact point. Do not fix this by simply blurring the whole shadow buffer — contact points must stay tight.
findings.hypothesis: The near cascade may be covering far more world area than its texel budget supports, or PCF may be sampling at exactly one tap. Both are cheap to check by reading the cascade split distances against the shadow map dimension and computing world-metres-per-texel for the near cascade; if that number is under 4 cm the cascade is not the cause and the aliasing is coming from somewhere else.

findings.problem: The anti-solar sky is a flat neutral grey card. In `phone-hero-r9.png` a column scan at x=2400 from y=30 to y=405 moves from 151,155,155 to 157,165,159 to 162,163,155 — a total vertical gradient of about 10 luma over 375 px, with R, G and B within 10 of each other at every sample. Box (1250,60 400x120) measures saturation 0.158 with detail 0.65; box (1400,200 300x150) measures saturation 0.092 with detail 1.00 and a p50-to-p99 spread of only 13 luma. In `phone-torii-r9.png` the sky above the range at (1700,60 200x60) is 118.8,147.4,162.9 (sat 0.271, lumaSpread 3.4) and near the horizon at (1700,560 200x60) it is 142.1,154.3,153.3 (sat 0.127) — green-grey, not the amber-to-indigo band a 13-degree sun produces. The sky occupies roughly a third of both frames and carries no cloud form anywhere in it (detail 0.56-1.00 over 300x80 and 400x120 boxes).
findings.why: The `sun` frame proves the sky model can produce a beautiful warm gradient when the sun is in shot. Turn 120 degrees away and it becomes an overcast studio backdrop, which flatly contradicts the golden-hour lighting on the ground and makes `hero` and `torii` read as an overcast afternoon with a strangely orange sun. Tsushima's signature torii approach is sold by the sky doing half the work — a deep saturated band at altitude, a hot band at the horizon, and cloud structure to give the eye scale.
findings.fix: On `phone-hero-r9.png`, box (1400,200 300x150) must reach saturation >= 0.28 (currently 0.092) and the x=2400 column from y=30 to y=405 must span >= 45 luma (currently ~10) with a monotonic warm shift toward the horizon — blue channel dominant at the top of frame, red channel dominant within 80 px of the horizon. Cloud form: at least one 400x120 sky box in `hero` must measure detail >= 4.0 from cloud structure alone (currently 0.65). Do not achieve this by raising exposure; re-measure the same boxes.
findings.hypothesis: Aerial/haze may be being applied to the sky dome itself as well as to geometry, washing the gradient toward a single grey before it reaches the frame. Testable in one pass: render the sky dome with the haze/fog term forced off and re-measure (1400,200 300x150). If saturation stays under 0.12 the haze is not the cause and the sky's own colour model is flat.

findings.problem: `phone-valley-r9.png` is a single-hue frame. Six 300x150 boxes spread across the entire image all return the same hue ordering with almost the same angle: (200,250) 126.8,99.2,51.2; (1200,300) 164.9,120.2,59.3; (2100,350) 69.3,52.1,31.0; (300,800) 76.7,42.8,20.1; (1900,900) 26.3,14.6,5.5; (1100,1050) 85.7,55.4,37.2. Every one is R > G > B at roughly 30 degrees hue. Critically, (1200,300) is inside the bamboo grove — the only green object in the shot — and it measures amber, 164.9,120.2,59.3. Whole-frame saturation is 0.610 with mean RGB 106.6,79.0,49.0. The deepest shadow in the frame, (1900,900), is still R:B = 4.8:1, so this is not sun-side forward scatter; it reaches the parts of the frame the sun cannot see.
findings.why: A monochrome amber frame has no palette, only a filter. The brief calls this accidental mud, and it is the difference between a colour grade and an Instagram preset. Sekiro's Ashina at dusk is amber and teal and moss simultaneously; strip the second and third hue and you get a frame a stranger describes as 'the orange one'.
findings.fix: The bamboo grove must survive as a distinguishable hue. Target: box (1200,300 300x150) in `valley` must return green channel >= red channel (currently 120.2 vs 164.9), and across the six boxes listed above at least two distinct hue families must be present — measure by computing hue angle per box and requiring a spread >= 45 degrees (currently under 12). Whole-frame saturation should stay in the 0.45-0.55 band; do not fix this by desaturating everything.
findings.hypothesis: Two candidates, and they are separable. Either the grade LUT/tint is being applied at near-full strength with no hue preservation, or the distance haze colour is being mixed in at a much shorter range in `valley` than in `wide` (the same bamboo band in `wide` at (760,340 300x120) measures 116.3,110.1,91.7, R and G within 6 of each other, i.e. far less hue collapse at 1000 m than `valley` shows at 40 m). Compare the two frames' haze start distance first; if they are identical, the grade is the cause.

findings.problem: The cherry blossom is orange and it is built from hard-edged polygon shards. Colour: in `hero` the canopy overall (180,90 480x330) is 122.1,84.1,74.4; a lit cluster at (420,165 40x30) is 84.8,50.0,48.3 and a shaded one at (300,300 40x30) is 70.8,43.2,43.5 — blue sits at 57-61% of red, which is brick, not pink. In `wide` it is worse: (950,880 200x100) = 78.7,39.3,27.6, blue at 35% of red, a pure flame orange; in the 1:1 crop of that region it reads as a small fire on the roof, not a tree. Form: a 1:1 crop of (250,150 400x250) shows the canopy is a mass of 20-50 px quadrilaterals with straight edges, flat interiors and hard black gaps between them. There is no petal-scale detail, no soft alpha edge and no translucency anywhere in the canopy; the unlit shards read as dead leaves or bark chips.
findings.why: Sakura is the single most recognisable silhouette in this genre and the one asset a viewer will compare directly against the reference without being asked. Tsushima's pink is a high-chroma accent deliberately held against cool blue; ours has neither the hue nor the softness, so at native resolution the hero tree reads as autumn debris and in `wide` it reads as an explosion.
findings.fix: Two targets. (1) Hue: the lit cluster box (420,165 40x30) in `hero` must return a blue channel >= 78% of its red channel (currently 57%), and `wide` (950,880 200x100) must reach >= 65% (currently 35%). Check whether the pink survives the tone map by sampling the same cluster before and after grading. (2) Form: the canopy needs blossom-scale breakup. Target on the (250,150 400x250) crop: no single flat-interior facet wider than 12 px should be visible, and the canopy's alpha edge against the sky must show >= 3 px of soft falloff rather than a 1 px cut. Do not solve this by shrinking the cards — that just makes smaller shards.
findings.hypothesis: The blossom cards may be carrying a single flat albedo with no per-petal alpha texture, so the only variation in the canopy is per-card lighting. Cheap to check: sample 20 pixels inside one card and see whether they differ by more than a few units.

findings.problem: The distant mountain range is a row of untextured paper triangles. A 1:1 crop of (1700,640 560x200) in `phone-torii-r9.png` shows four near-identical pale triangles with dead-straight edges and uniform fill. Measured on the peak body at (2030,700 70x40): detail 2.02, lumaSpread 33.5, saturation 0.102, mean 165.9,158.2,149.1. Another at (2000,560 80x40): detail 0.88, lumaSpread 21.7, saturation 0.078 — that is mean absolute Laplacian under 1.0 over a 3200 px region, i.e. essentially no surface variation at all, against 8.31 measured on the courtyard ground in the same frame. There is no snow line, no ridge structure, no rock, and no warm/cool split despite a 13-degree sun.
findings.why: Priority 5 in the brief. A 1.8 km view whose far range has no internal form is a painted backdrop, and the four repeated triangle shapes make the repetition legible. Tsushima's distant ranges carry visible ridge lines and a clear sunward/shadow split even through heavy haze — that is what convinces the eye there is real space between the camera and the horizon.
findings.fix: Target on `phone-torii-r9.png`: the peak body box (2030,700 70x40) must reach detail >= 5.5 (currently 2.02) and lumaSpread >= 55 (currently 33.5) from ridge and snow-line structure, and the sunward flank of any peak must be measurably warmer than its shaded flank — sample matched 40x40 boxes either side of a summit and require a red-minus-blue difference of >= 12 between them (currently the whole peak is within 17 of neutral). The four peaks must not be congruent silhouettes.
findings.hypothesis: The far range may be a separate low-detail proxy mesh from the macro heightfield that produces the textured massif in `wide` (which measures detail 4.3-5.39 at (900,200) and (1400,220)), rather than the same system at greater distance. Worth confirming which mesh draws those pixels before touching either.

findings.problem: Every lit lantern clips to a neutral white rectangle and emits no light into the scene. In `phone-hero-r9.png` a row scan at y=800 through the stone lantern reads 251,249,242 at x=1620 — an achromatic white core, saturation ~0.04 — with the surrounding paper at (1608,780 26x40) only reaching 177.4,151.9,124.5. Falloff is nil: at x=1660, 40 px from the panel, the value is already 50,20,4, and at x=1670 it is 106,75,59, which is plain ambient. Ground under the lantern (1560,1090 90x40) measures 51.0,31.4,20.0 against ground 340 px away (1900,1090 90x40) at 36.7,24.4,19.2 — a 1.4x difference that is fully explained by the sun gradient, so there is no light pool. Same in `torii`: both lantern panels in the 1:1 crop of (1650,500 880x440) are flat cream rectangles with hard borders and no halo, and the stone posts they sit on are unlit.
findings.why: In Sekiro a lantern is the warmest, most saturated object in the frame and it pools light on its own post and the ground around it — that pool is what makes a shrine approach at dusk feel lit rather than decorated. Ours are white stickers. Worse, an achromatic core on a flame-lit paper shade is the classic over-driven-emissive tell: the highlight has been pushed past the tone map shoulder until all hue is gone.
findings.fix: The panel core must stay chromatic. Target on `phone-hero-r9.png`: the brightest pixel of the lantern paper near (1620,800) must retain saturation >= 0.25 (currently ~0.04) while staying under 250 luma — roughly 250,200,130 rather than 251,249,242. Separately, the lantern must contribute light: the ground box (1560,1090 90x40) should read at least 2.2x the luma of (1900,1090 90x40) with a visibly warmer bias, and the stone post immediately below each panel must show a warm gradient falling off over 1-2 m rather than the flat value it has now.
findings.hypothesis: The emissive may be authored as an unlit constant that is neither wavelength-weighted nor feeding any light source, so it survives tone mapping as clipped white and never reaches the shading of anything else. If a point/spot light already exists at each lantern, check its measured contribution by ablating it and re-measuring (1560,1090) — if the number does not move, the light is not linked.

findings.problem: The village reads as a level editor, not a place. A 1:1 crop of (1150,640 500x280) shows identical stone lantern posts at a regular pitch along a straight line, all the same height, all perfectly vertical, all the same material, with nothing between them. The ground they stand on is a uniform plane: box (1100,850 300x120) measures mean 73.8,48.2,33.6 with detail 9.60, and that detail is entirely small-scale texture noise — there is no path, no worn track, no grass tuft, no debris, no puddle, no large-scale value variation anywhere in the courtyard. Nothing in the frame is broken, tilted, weathered differently from its neighbour, or placed asymmetrically.
findings.why: Priority 8. Real shrine approaches accumulate: some lanterns lean, some are moss-stained, the path between them is worn to a lighter track, offerings and leaf litter collect at the bases. Perfect repetition at a constant pitch is the strongest single signal that props were placed by a loop rather than by a person, and it is legible even at contact-sheet size.
findings.fix: Break the array. On `phone-wide-r9.png` in the region x 1150-1650, y 640-920: lantern post spacing must vary by at least +/-25%, heights by at least +/-15%, and at least one in four posts should carry a visible tilt, a different weathering value, or an accumulation at its base. Separately the ground needs large-scale variation: a worn path along the lantern line should read as a measurably different value from the ground either side — target a >= 25% luma difference between a 100x60 box on the path and one 200 px off it, where currently the difference is under 5%.
findings.hypothesis: None offered — this is a placement/dressing call, not a shading one.

findings.problem: `phone-valley-r9.png` has no composition. Ground fills the bottom 60% of the frame as a single unbroken plane, the bamboo wall runs across the top as a single unbroken band, and the only object in the shot is a fence at the very bottom edge. There is no foreground element framing the view, no mid-ground subject, and no silhouette worth reading — squint and the frame reduces to two horizontal stripes. Whole-frame detail is 7.54 but it is uniformly distributed; there is no point of interest for the eye to land on.
findings.why: Priority 4. Every other framing in the set has at least a torii or a roofline to hang the shot on; this one is a texture swatch with a fence in it, and on the contact sheet it is the frame that most obviously does not belong in a store page.
findings.fix: Re-frame so the shot has three depths. Put a real occluding element in the near field — a bamboo culm cluster, a torii leg, a rock — occupying 15-25% of frame area on one third line, keep a readable subject in the mid-ground, and let the grove and light shafts be the background. Verify by checking that a 400x400 box on the near third measures a luma p50 at least 30% below the mid-ground, so the frame has an actual foreground rather than a continuous ramp.
findings.hypothesis: None offered — this is a camera placement call.
